lines.note: Torisoroye means gathering things together or putting them in order; the Portuguese gives joining or equalizing them. The scan contains the ordinary initial T omitted by OCR; it is not an enlarged initial.

Taru and sakana name the wine vessels and accompanying food that are being arranged. Torisoroyuru is the historical finite form corresponding to the headword, and igualar completes the preceding Portuguese alternative.

runs.text: Por por ordẽ as barças de vinho, & Sacanas.

lines.note: The Portuguese explains arranging the wine vessels and sakana in order. Sacanas is a Japanese food term embedded in the Portuguese sentence; its printed plural ending and italic setting are retained.
Torisoye means adding or taking something together with another item. The following illustration specifies a vessel and its accompanying drinking cup; Acrecẽtar retains the printed abbreviation.

runs.text: couſa, & outra como o bule, & taça, ou copo.

lines.note: The paired objects are the bule and a taça or copo, a pot and a drinking vessel. This completes the idea of taking two associated objects together, rather than introducing another entry.
Torisucume is glossed as forcing or constraining. The Portuguese conſtrãger is abbreviated in print and is preserved without supplying the missing nasal letter.
Torisute means throwing or casting away. The historical principal form tçuru belongs to this verb and should not be replaced by a modern teru form.
Com a mão specifies casting something away by hand and completes the preceding definition. The short continuation is an independent physical row.
Toritate first means building or raising houses. The following rows extend the verb to restoring or advancing a person socially.

runs.text: caſas. ¶ Item, Tornar por a alguem no ſeu

lines.note: After completing caſas, the gloss adds restoring someone to his own former condition. Tornar belongs to the Portuguese italic explanation, including its capital T.
The example begins hito no ie wo toritatsuru, concerning raising a person’s house or household. Proprio eſtado completes the preceding statement about restoring his position.
Tçuru completes toritatsuru; the Portuguese gloss explains raising someone and setting him on his feet. The expression therefore allows a social or household sense as well as literal construction.
The gloss continues with improving someone’s station. Hito wo tori- begins the next example, whose final verb continues on the following row.

runs.text: Armar a alguem, ou fazelo homẽ.

lines.note: Tatçuru completes hito wo toritatsuru. Armar a alguem and fazelo homẽ describe establishing or making someone into a person of standing; the abbreviated homẽ is retained.

runs.text: O edificar. ¶ Item, O fazer a

lines.note: The noun toritate denotes the act of building and then the act of establishing another person. It is a separate nominal entry following the verb.

runs.text: alguem homem, ou pollo com eſtado. ¶

lines.note: The gloss explains making someone a man of standing or setting him up in an estate or position. A- starts ano in the Japanese example below.
Ano hito wa waga toritate ja means that the person owes his establishment to the speaker. Aquelle he fei- begins the Portuguese equivalent across the physical line break.

runs.text: tura minha. i, Eu o fiz homem.

lines.note: Tura completes feitura: that person is the speaker’s creation or protégé. Eu o fiz homem explicitly explains the sense as having established him.
Toritsukami means grasping or seizing something. The scan has two r types in Afferrar; the principal part ǒda retains its caron and historical contracted inflection.
Couſa completes the object of afferrar de algũa, grasping something. It is the genuine short closing row of this entry.
Toritsukuroi means arranging or preparing something properly. The printed ô and ôta principal parts use circumflexes, unlike the caron in the preceding entry.

runs.text: lhar bem, & polidamente quer ſeja vestido,

lines.note: The explanation adds that the arrangement is neat and polished, whether the object is clothing or the room mentioned next. The inherited vestido reading is retained without globally changing the difficult italic st class.

Zaxiqu denotes zashiki, a room or reception space, within the Portuguese explanation and remains italic as printed. Enlargement shows no independent final i after the u before the comma; retain this shortened or damaged form with a nonblocking caveat. The new Japanese example begins toritsukurōta furumai, a carefully arranged banquet, across the break.
Rumai completes furumai. The Portuguese Conuite describes a banquet or entertainment that has been properly arranged and prepared; the scan supports n rather than the OCR’s m.
Relhado completes aparelhado, prepared or furnished. This finishes the banquet example rather than starting a new sense.
Toritsugi as a verb means mediating or passing on a message. The next line specifies that the message or information is delivered to a lord.

runs.text: recado, ou parte a algum ſenhor do que lhe tra-

lines.note: The intermediary gives a lord notice of what people bring or send to him. The final tra- continues as trazem on the next row.

runs.text: zem, ou mandão dizer. ¶ Item, Alicu-

lines.note: Zem completes trazem, and mandão dizer means sending word. The scan supports dizer rather than OCR drzer; Alicu- begins the restricted-local-use label alicubi.

runs.text: bi, Socorrer com mantimẽto, ou prata. Meliùs,

lines.note: Bi completes alicubi, introducing a locally used sense of supplying someone with provisions or silver. Meliùs then introduces the preferred Japanese expression on the next line.

The cross-reference denotes continuing support, corresponding to toritsuzukuru. The print reads Tori çuzzuquru, with a space and no securely visible t before ç; retain this anomalous form instead of silently supplying the expected letter.

runs.text: Medianeiro, ou o que falla por

lines.note: The noun toritsugi denotes an intermediary or spokesman. The relative clause continues with when and before whom he speaks.

runs.text: alguem a ſeus tẽpos diante do ſenhor. ¶

lines.note: The intermediary speaks for someone at the appropriate times before the lord. To- begins the illustrative toritsugi wo suru phrase.
Ritçuguiuo ſuru completes toritsugi wo suru, acting as an intermediary. The Portuguese repeats that meaning and begins intercessor across the line break.
Terceßor completes interceßor, an intercessor or mediator. The visible ß-shaped type is retained in this short continuation.
Toritsume is explained as putting something under pressure or in a strait. Xi- begins shiro, the fortress in the example below.
Shiro wo toritsumuru means pressing or closely besieging a fortress. The Portuguese for- begins fortaleza on the next physical row.
Taleza completes fortaleza, the object placed under pressure. The full short continuation belongs to the siege example.
Toritsuke here means taking hold and attaching or adding something. Tomando is part of the italic Portuguese gloss; its capital is not a separate Japanese item.
The example combines toritsuke and hittsuke with mono wo yuu, describing speech that adds things together. The final verb is continued on the following row.

runs.text: Falar acrecentando de cà, & de là.

lines.note: Yǔ completes the Japanese example. The Portuguese explains adding material from here and there while speaking, retaining the printed grave accents in cà and là.
Toritsuki means clinging or taking firm hold. The uita principal part is retained as the dictionary’s historical notation, rather than expanded or modernized.
Hito no te ni toritsuku illustrates grasping someone’s hand. Vt introduces the example and remains italic; the Japanese phrase is upright.

runs.text: Pegar, ou afferrar da mão dalguem. ¶

lines.note: The Portuguese translates the hand-grasping example. Tẽ- begins tengu with an abbreviation tilde, and belongs wholly to the upright Japanese phrase, not partly to the italic gloss.
Tenguga hito ni toritsuku describes a tengu attaching itself to or possessing a person. The dictionary renders this as the devil entering someone; the continuation supplies the final object.
Alguem completes the Portuguese explanation of possession. It is a short body-text continuation, not stray furniture.
Toritsutsumi means surrounding with people or troops. The final line lists the military or civic targets that can be encircled.
The examples are a fortress, an army, and a city. Enlarged inspection supports fortaleza and exercito, correcting the OCR’s ſortaleza and excreio without modernizing the spelling.
Toritsuzuke means causing something to continue. Vt introduces the military example on the next line; the principal forms are preserved as printed.
Jin wo toritsuzukuru describes extending the camp or military array. Estender and the divided dilatar give the corresponding Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: latar o arrayal. ¶ Item, Socorrer a alguẽ

lines.note: Latar completes dilatar o arrayal, extending the camp. A second sense then begins: supplying or assisting someone in a shortage.

runs.text: em algũa falta, ou neceßidade como de dinhei-

lines.note: The assistance addresses a lack or need, with money introduced as the first example. Dinhei- continues as dinheiro on the next physical line.
Ro completes dinheiro; rice is the other named provision. The row finishes the material-support sense rather than adding a new headword.
Toritsuzuki is the intransitive counterpart, continuing without interruption. The following row completes the Portuguese word for interval.
Tervallo completes enteruallo: without an interval. This short row remains separate from the next Buddhist name.
Tōriten names a heaven, as the concise Portuguese definition states. The printed caron in Tǒriten is retained; the entry is distinct from the later two tōryū words.
Toritome means detaining someone by taking hold of him. The construction pegando delle is completed on the following line.
Delle completes the physical-detaining gloss. Toritomete mono wo suru then illustrates another use, doing something with care and concentration.

runs.text: zer algũa couſa com diligencia, & cuidado.

lines.note: The translation specifies diligence and care in doing something. This completes the toritomete example without adding a separate noun entry.

runs.text: O que caça, ou toma paßaros.

lines.note: Tori tori is a person who catches or hunts birds. The repeated tori sequence is meaningful and must not be collapsed as duplicated OCR.
Tori torimochi is birdlime used for catching birds. The compound and the preceding bird-catcher entry have different referents despite their shared opening.
Toritouonoqi means drawing away or becoming distant. The Portuguese gives alongar-se and begins afastar-se at the line end.
Fastarſe longe completes the alternative explanation, moving far away. The inherited st reading is retained without a conjectural allograph change.
Tôriǔ denotes a stay or delay, and Tôriǔ suru means remaining or delaying. The scan supports r, correcting OCR Tôniǔ; the circumflex over o contrasts with the following headword’s caron.
Se completes deter-se, followed by fazer detença, making a stay. It completes the first tōryū entry, not the next entry about a currently prevalent school.

runs.text: Eſta arte, ou doutrina, ou ley que a-

lines.note: Tǒriǔ denotes the current school, teaching, or tradition. The initial is T, not OCR r; enlarged inspection confirms the caron, distinguishing this entry from Tôriǔ above. The supplied NINJAL v202510 index also lists the two separately.
Gora completes agora: the art, doctrine, or law currently in circulation. This short ending is part of the current-school definition.
Toriwake and toriwaki are given as adverbial alternatives meaning particularly. The lowercase l is Latin vel, introducing an alternative rather than forming part of a Japanese word.
Larmente completes particularmente, particularly or especially. It closes the adverbial entry before the separate verb toriwake.
Toriwake as a verb is explained here as taking half of something. The historical quru principal form is preserved rather than replaced by modern keru.

runs.text: gũa couſa, ou partir pollo meo.

lines.note: The alternatives are taking half or dividing through the middle. Pollo meo is retained as the printed Portuguese construction.
Toriwatari means crossing the sea or a river, with the collective subject continued below. The scan’s single long s in Paſar is retained rather than regularized.
Muita gente supplies the people making the crossing. The short continuation is essential to the entry’s collective sense.

runs.text: Hũa parte do arco adiante donde o

lines.note: Toriuchi names part of a bow beyond the section held in the hand. The precise position is described through the next line, not replaced by a modern anatomical label.
The bow is grasped at its middle in the hand. This completes the relative location of the toriuchi part described above.
Toriwoconai means carrying out administration or governing. Both the principal forms and the repeated examples retain their printed open-long-o carons.
Matsurigoto wo toriwoconō illustrates conducting government or administering laws. The Portuguese Dar le- begins leis across the break.

Is completes leis and its governing gloss. Fōji wo toriwoconō supplies a second example, conducting a rite or religious observance, whose Portuguese translation occupies the previously omitted next row.

runs.text: Celebrar, ou fazer algum officio, ou ſolẽnidade.

lines.note: Celebrating or performing an office or solemn observance translates the preceding Fôjiuo torivoconǒ example. This complete physical row was absent from the OCR draft; the printed ſolẽnidade retains its abbreviation tilde.
Toriwoki means putting away and keeping something in its proper place. A second sense involving burial follows in the same entry.
After completing the keeping-in-place gloss, the entry adds burying the dead. Xi- begins shigai, a corpse, in the example.
Gaiuo torivoqu completes shigai wo toriwoku, burying or putting away a corpse. The short Japanese continuation remains upright and is not Portuguese commentary.
Toriwosame means putting inside or burying. The following rows add storage in a granary as another specific application.
Terrar completes enterrar. Enceleirar introduces storing in a granary; Nengu- begins the example involving the land levy.
Nengu wo toriwosamuru means collecting or storing the land revenue. The Portuguese recolher and enceleirar give those two related actions.
O rendimento das terras identifies the land income or levy being collected. It completes the example and is not a separate tax headword.
Toriwotoshi first means failing or leaving something untaken. The oita principal part belongs to the historical s-verb inflection and is not silently changed to modern oshita.

runs.text: tomar algũa couſa por eſquecimento. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: The omission occurs through forgetfulness. Itẽ then introduces a second sense involving an object slipping or falling from the hand.

runs.text: Cair algũa couſa da mão que ſe tomaua, ou hia

lines.note: The second sense is something falling from the hand while being taken or about to be taken. Hia fits the historical Portuguese construction; its initial resembles b, but comparison with the similarly closed italic h in homem at c1-l018 supports h. This h/b identification remains a nonblocking uncertainty.
Pera ſe tomar completes the phrase about an object that was going to be taken. It belongs to the falling-object sense rather than the following falconry verb.
Torishiki describes a falcon taking a bird. The printed qu, ijta principal parts are retained; the next line specifies where the capture occurs.
Entre as eruas means among the grass or vegetation. It completes the falconry definition, not another Japanese example.
Torishitatame means arranging or putting something in order. The Portuguese final cou continues as couſa on the next row without a clearly printed hyphen.

runs.text: ſa como cama, ou fato que ſe amarra, ou

lines.note: Examples include bedding and belongings or cloth tied into a bundle. The initial ſa completes couſa from the preceding physical row.

runs.text: outra couſa que ſe poem em ſeu lugar. ¶

lines.note: The definition extends to any other thing put in its proper place. Fu- begins fumi in the example continued on the next page; the separate miuo below is a catchword repeating the next page’s opening, not an extra body row.
